What counts as hacking

Internet hacking is the unauthorized access, manipulation, or exploitation of digital devices, computer systems, and network connections. It happens when someone finds and uses a weakness in software, hardware, or human behavior to steal data, disrupt services, or take control of a system.

#1

Infcurion Wallet Station (payment app platform, Japan; Payどん, AEON Pay)

HighFinanceTech🇯🇵JP
Nov 19, 2026Updated Nov 21
Threat
Up to about250,000users

Japanese fintech Infcurion says a third party broke into Wallet Station, the platform companies use to run their own smartphone payment apps, and personal data of app users leaked. It detected a flood of access on the night of Nov. 19, blocked the attacker's traffic, applied an emergency vulnerability patch and cut off service to the affected clients.

Impact

Up to about 250,000 users' records. Payどん, the Kagoshima payment app run by four local banks, says 251,172 records leaked, including names, birth dates, email addresses, passwords, account information, point balances and transaction history; it stopped all services on the morning of Nov. 20. AEON Pay suspended some code payments and donations during emergency maintenance but says it has found no leak of its customers' data.

Status

Confirmed by Infcurion and the Payどん banks. Infcurion says there has been no new unauthorized access since it blocked the attacker on Nov. 19 and no misuse of the leaked data so far. From Nov. 20 it paused Wallet Station for its other clients for emergency checks; those checked so far showed no intrusion or leak and began restarting on Nov. 21, while service for the affected clients stays suspended with no restart date.

Customer messaging platform MoEngage says that in late October an attacker used a compromised third-party vendor account to get into a limited part of its cloud infrastructure. #4

Microsoft Entra Connect Health (tenant metadata exposure)

MediumTech🇺🇸US
Nov 9, 2026Updated Nov 21
Threat

Microsoft notified affected organizations that unauthorized parties exploited a vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API, a cloud service admins use to monitor on-premises identity infrastructure. The flaw was introduced on July 23, 2026, and Microsoft discovered it on Nov. 9.

Impact

Read-only access to tenant-level metadata, including email addresses of tenant technical contacts and administrator accounts, tenant IDs, display names, initial domains, country codes, license tiers, directory sync status and an expired certificate. Microsoft says no passwords, password hashes, authentication tokens, valid keys or Azure subscription data were exposed, and it found no unauthorized configuration changes. It has not said how many organizations were affected.

Status

Confirmed by Microsoft in notifications to affected tenants. A server-side fix was deployed Nov. 19 and the investigation concluded Nov. 20; no customer action is required to fix the flaw, but admins are urged to watch for targeted phishing.

#7

PLAID KARTE customers (MUFG Bank, JINS, Shimamura and others, Japan)

CriticalTechFinanceRetail🇯🇵JP
Nov 13, 2026Updated Nov 20
Threat

Attackers exploited a vulnerability in servers run by PLAID, the Tokyo company behind the KARTE customer-data marketing service, stole credentials used to connect to its systems and databases, and read data out. They also took over a PLAID account to get into the admin console. PLAID shut down all KARTE services on Nov. 13, and companies that use KARTE have been announcing leaks of their own customers' data since. On Nov. 20 PLAID said about 2,200 client companies in total (counting overlaps) had data leaked or possibly leaked.

Impact

Varies by company. MUFG Bank: about 6.5 million records of gender, age and region (no names or contact details). JINS: up to about 18.29 million accounts (email, surname, birth date and more). Shimamura: about 7 million members' birth dates, gender, prefecture and postal code. RIZAP: up to about 4.32 million email addresses. J.League: about 2.38 million ticketing records (internal user IDs, birth dates, gender, prefecture and city). Stripe International: about 150,000 STRIPE CLUB records with email addresses and member IDs. Wacoal: internal IDs, ages, birth dates and gender possibly leaked (count still under investigation). NTT Solmare: up to about 1.17 million MangaPlaza records and up to about 130,000 Comic Cmoa records (hashed member numbers, birth dates, gender and more). Sharp: up to about 3.26 million online store customers' ages, birth dates and other details (NHK). Uniform Next: up to about 1.7 million customer records (company names, names, email addresses, phone numbers, postal codes, job types and industries; no passwords, card data or addresses). Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp. (SMBC): up to about 14 million records of birth dates, gender and whether a phone number is registered (not linked to names; Nikkei). Goldwin: about 3.67 million Goldwin Members email addresses, birth dates, gender, prefecture and activity data (no names, card data or passwords). Mainichi Shimbun: about 140,000 Mainichi Shimbun Digital members' surnames, plus ages, plan names, point-club IDs or email addresses for some. ZOZO: about 15.18 million ZOZOTOWN and 13.93 million WEAR member records (see separate entry). Tokyo Gas also confirmed customer data leaked, with numbers still under investigation. PLAID also says credentials used to link KARTE to outside services leaked, and has asked customers to revoke them.

Status

Confirmed by PLAID and affected companies. PLAID says about 2,200 client companies (2,220 counting overlaps) may be affected, including 570 whose linked customer data may have leaked; it plans to give clients detailed data from Nov. 24, expects to restart KARTE in mid-January, and now forecasts a full-year net loss of about ¥2 billion (Nikkei).

Status

Confirmed by Yumir Link and affected clients. Yumir Link says it was not ransomware and most services are running again; final investigation results pending. Peach reported to Japan's privacy regulator and is notifying customers.

Ransomware network extorting U.S. firms (Ukraine arrests)

HighEnergyManufacturingHealthcare🇺🇸US
Nov 18, 2026Updated Nov 20
Threat

Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office, working with the FBI, said police arrested four suspected key members of a ransomware group of at least 27 people, part of a wider network of more than 60 that includes former Conti members. Police say the group posed as IT support to trick employees into handing over logins or installing remote access tools, then stole data and encrypted systems. Ukrainian authorities have since linked the four to the Chaos ransomware operation, which Computer Weekly reports grew out of the Royal/BlackSuit lineage; they are accused of a 2024 attack on Maxxis under the BlackSuit name before switching to Chaos.

Impact

Authorities say at least 28 companies were extorted for a combined $40.5 million. Ukrainian court records name U.S. targets including Warren Oil, Maxxis International-USA, Newpark Resources and Quantum Health (The Record). Court documents describe ransoms of about $11.5 million across the Maxxis, Newpark and Warren Oil attacks (Computer Weekly).

Status

Confirmed by Ukrainian law enforcement. Four suspects held in pretrial detention, expected until Jan. 1, with bail set for three; they face up to 15 years in prison. 66 searches carried out and cash, devices and bank cards seized.

In the early hours of Nov. 2, a second wave of attacks hit internet-connected refrigeration controls at supermarkets and food businesses in at least 10 European countries, switching fridges and freezers into defrost mode. Around 40 Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg and 13 SuperValu stores in Ireland were among those hit, and three British meat suppliers were affected through vulnerable Copeland XWEB controllers.

Impact

Freezer temperatures reportedly rose as high as 50C, forcing retailers to throw away food. In the UK, the affected meat suppliers' units were empty, so no meat was lost. Status

Confirmed as cyberattacks by affected companies, including Sabcobel (which runs Delhaize's systems) and SuperValu owner Musgrave. Belgian federal prosecutors are investigating. No one has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not attributed this wave.

#2

Threat

The National Security Agency's internal top-secret network, NSANet, went down right on the heels of a week of big outages and stayed disrupted for nearly four days. It was restored on Nov. 20.

What people speculated

An attack on a U.S. intelligence network.

Official explanation

The NSA described it as scheduled maintenance. Multiple U.S. officials told CNN it was not a cyberattack and appears tied to the agency's patching of recently disclosed vulnerabilities in PHP software; a senior administration official said the restoration work was going "slower than expected." At a Nov. 18 House hearing, U.S. intelligence and FBI officials said they had seen no indication of malicious cyber activity in the recent outages.

Impact

Large parts of the NSA workforce sent home for days. The outage also hit NSA Georgia, which supports Middle East operations; officials say the agency's most sensitive intelligence systems kept working and backups were used. On Nov. 20 NSA told staff it was operating under "normal conditions with exceptions," with staggered building openings to avoid a login surge.

Status

Network restored Nov. 20. Officials attribute it to patching problems; no evidence of a hack.

About and methodology

How confirmed and speculated are decided

  • Confirmed Hacks were confirmed by the affected organization, a government agency, or law enforcement. Numbers come from those statements, filings, or the linked reporting. Attacker claims are labeled as claims.
  • Speculated / Potential Hacks are outages or incidents where the public wondered about a hack. They are not confirmed hacks. Each one shows what the organization or investigators officially said.

How this tracker is updated

  • The list is reviewed and updated about every two hours during the day, Eastern Time.
  • Sorted by the most recent incident or news update first. An older entry that gets new information moves back up. Severity is a rough editorial rating, not an official score.
  • The lists default to incidents that affected U.S. organizations or people. Use the USA / Worldwide switch to see the full list.
  • Covers roughly the past 12 months, plus a few older events that are still widely referenced. Always check the linked sources for the latest.

The definition of hacking used on this site is at the top of the page, under What counts as hacking.
